metadata.pmid_attribution: Data sourced from PubMed articles. All PMIDs reference peer-reviewed literature retrieved from PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/).

muscle_injury.name: British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC)
muscle_injury.basis: MRI - injury location within muscle (a=myofascial, b=muscle belly, c=musculotendinous junction) and severity

muscle_injury.name: Munich Consensus Injury Classification (MCIC)
muscle_injury.basis: MRI - structural vs. functional, anatomical location

ligament_injury.name: Standard Ligament Sprain Classification
grades: Grade 1 (mild stretch, microscopic tears, full strength)

bone_stress.name: MRI Grading for Bone Stress Injuries
grades: Grade 1: periosteal edema on fat-suppressed MRI, no cortical signal abnormality
Grade 2: periosteal edema + medullary signal change, no fracture line
Grade 3: periosteal edema + medullary signal + cortical involvement
Grade 4: fracture line visible on MRI

ankle_sprain_ottawa.name: Ottawa Ankle Rules
ankle_sprain_ottawa.description: Clinical decision tool for excluding fractures after ankle sprain
criteria: Bone tenderness at posterior tip or distal 6cm of fibula
Bone tenderness at posterior tip or distal 6cm of tibia
Inability to bear weight immediately and in ED
Bone tenderness at navicular or base of 5th metatarsal

grades.description: BAMIC 1a/1b: Mild myofascial or muscle belly injury, minimal fiber disruption (<5%), intact architecture
BAMIC 2a/2b/2c: Moderate partial tear, significant fiber disruption, possible musculotendinous junction involvement
BAMIC 3a/3b/3c or 4: Severe partial-to-complete tear, may involve intramuscular tendon; each BAMIC grade increase = ~3 additional days recovery

high_sensitivity: Posterior thigh pain during or immediately after sprinting
Tenderness on palpation of posterior thigh
Pain with resisted knee flexion
Pain with passive hip flexion + knee extended (active slump)
high_specificity: MRI signal change on fat-suppressed sequences
Ultrasound confirmation of fiber disruption
BAMIC grading by radiologist (Kappa 0.506)
Pain on palpation at specific muscle belly vs. musculotendinous junction

sport_risk_factors: Previous hamstring injury (strongest predictor of re-injury)
Being removed from play rather than self-withdrawing

grades.description: Mild: minimal fiber disruption, localized anterior thigh pain, full strength
Moderate: partial tear, significant pain with resisted knee extension, palpable defect possible
Severe: complete or near-complete tear, significant functional deficit, may require surgical consultation

mechanisms: Overstretch with hip extended and knee flexed

high_sensitivity: Anterior thigh pain with resisted knee extension
Tenderness on palpation of quadriceps bulk
Pain with passive knee flexion (stretch)
high_specificity: MRI/ultrasound confirming fiber disruption at rectus femoris or vastus intermedius
BAMIC or MCIC classification via imaging

grades.description: Partial ACL tear: some fibers intact, minimal laxity, no complete instability
Significant partial tear: increased laxity, functional instability in high-demand activities
Complete rupture: gross instability, positive pivot shift, typically requires reconstruction; return 9-12 months post-surgery

mechanisms: Non-contact: valgus collapse during landing or cutting (most common female mechanism)
Contact: valgus force at knee (tackle, collision)
Rotational force during change of direction

high_sensitivity: Acute onset knee pain with audible pop
Rapid hemarthrosis (within 2 hours)
Subjective giving way or instability
Positive Lachman test (>3mm anterior translation)
high_specificity: Positive pivot shift test (pathognomonic for ACL deficiency)
MRI T2 signal change at ACL
Dynamic ultrasound Lachman (cutoff 2.6mm: sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%)

sport_risk_factors: Female athletes (2-8x higher risk than males)

grades.description: Mild stretch: microscopic tears, no laxity, localized medial joint tenderness
Partial tear: moderate laxity with firm endpoint, significant pain. HBO2 group return ~31 days vs 42 days standard care
Complete rupture: gross valgus laxity, no endpoint; may require surgery if combined with ACL injury

mechanisms: Direct valgus blow to lateral knee (most common)

high_sensitivity: Medial joint line tenderness on palpation
Pain with valgus stress at 30 degrees knee flexion
Swelling over medial aspect
high_specificity: Valgus stress test with measurable laxity (>3mm opening = Grade 2, no endpoint = Grade 3)
MRI confirms location: superficial vs. deep MCL

grades.description: Grade 1 MRI: intrasubstance signal change not reaching articular surface (often incidental)
Grade 2 MRI: horizontal or linear signal not reaching surface
Grade 3 MRI: signal reaching articular surface = true tear; classified by pattern (vertical, horizontal, radial, complex, root tear)

mechanisms: Degenerative: repetitive loading, no specific incident
Combined ACL injury (associated medial meniscus tear)

high_sensitivity: Joint line tenderness (medial or lateral)
Pain with deep knee flexion
Locking or catching sensation
Delayed swelling (6-24 hours post-injury)
high_specificity: McMurray test positive (click/pain with rotation)
Thessaly test at 20 degrees
MRI Grade 3 signal at appropriate meniscal zone

grades.description: Blazina Stage 1: Pain only after activity, does not interfere with performance
Blazina Stage 2: Pain at beginning and after activity, satisfactory performance maintained
Blazina Stage 3: Pain during and after activity, unable to perform; VISA-P score <40/100 indicates severe impairment

high_sensitivity: Proximal patellar tendon tenderness on palpation
Pain with single-leg squat
Pain with resisted knee extension
VISA-P score <80/100
high_specificity: Ultrasound: hypoechoic area at proximal patellar tendon
MRI: intrasubstance signal at proximal attachment
VISA-P reliability ICC = 0.94 (meta-analysis of 12 studies)

sport_risk_factors: Elite vs recreational athletes (higher risk elite)

grades.description: Mild: pain with prolonged activity only, no restriction of daily activities
Moderate: pain with moderate activity, some restriction; Kujala score 65-80
Severe: pain at rest or minimal activity; Kujala score <65; chondral changes may be present

mechanisms: Biomechanical: excessive contralateral pelvic drop (1 degree increase = 80% odds increase)
Weak hip abductors and external rotators

high_sensitivity: Anterior or retropatellar knee pain with activity
Pain worse on stairs, squatting, prolonged sitting
Peripatellar or retropatellar tenderness on palpation
Crepitus with knee movement
high_specificity: Patellar grind test positive
Clarke's sign (painful inhibition test)
Exclusion of other knee pathology (meniscal, ligamentous)

sport_risk_factors: Cycling (prepatellar friction most common ~46% of cyclists)

grades.description: Mild: pain after exercise only, does not limit activity
Moderate: pain during exercise, limits activity
Severe: pain with all activity including walking; chronic friction bursitis

mechanisms: Biomechanical: excessive contralateral pelvic drop, hip abductor weakness
Cambered road running (same side traffic exposure)

high_sensitivity: Lateral knee pain approximately 2-3 cm proximal to lateral joint line
Pain onset at consistent distance/time during run
Ober test positive for IT band tightness
high_specificity: Noble compression test (maximum tenderness at 30 degrees knee flexion)
MRI: signal change in IT band at lateral femoral condyle

sport_risk_factors: Cycling (3.7% of overuse knee injuries in cyclists)

grades.description: Grade I: ATFL stretch, minimal swelling, full weight-bearing, normal stress radiographs. Return to sport: days to 1 week
Grade II: Partial ATFL tear (+/- CFL), moderate swelling, pain with weight-bearing, mild laxity. Ottawa Rules negative for fracture typically
Grade IIIA/IIIB (expanded): Complete ATFL (+/- CFL) rupture. IIIA: <10 degrees talar tilt; IIIB: >10 degrees talar tilt or >3mm anterior drawer vs. contralateral

mechanisms: Landing from jump on uneven surface
Contact: player landing on another's foot

high_sensitivity: Lateral ankle pain after inversion mechanism
Swelling and ecchymosis over ATFL
Tenderness on palpation of anterior talofibular ligament
Ottawa Ankle Rules for excluding fracture (sensitivity 98%)
high_specificity: Anterior drawer test >3mm or >3mm vs. contralateral
Talar tilt test >10 degrees
Stress radiographs (if clinically indicated)
MRI if Grade III suspected or chronic instability

grades.description: Grade I: Sprain only, stable syndesmosis on stress radiograph
Grade II: Partial disruption, equivocal stability
Grade III: Complete disruption, tibiofibular diastasis on stress radiograph; often requires surgical stabilization. Chronic symptoms in 23.6% if untreated >2 months

mechanisms: External rotation of foot on planted ankle
Misidentified as lateral ankle sprain (incidence 1-16% of all ankle sprains)

high_sensitivity: Pain proximal to ankle joint (above lateral malleolus)
External rotation stress test positive
Squeeze test (proximal fibula compression) positive
Pain with dorsiflexion
high_specificity: Stress radiograph showing tibiofibular diastasis
MRI confirming interosseous membrane disruption
Cotton test (lateral drawer of fibula relative to tibia)

grades.description: Reactive/Early (VISA-A 70-100): pain only after activity, no structural change on imaging
Tendon dysrepair/Moderate (VISA-A 40-70): pain during and after activity, degenerative changes on ultrasound, Curwin-Stanish Grade 3-4
Degenerative (VISA-A <40): persistent pain limiting all sport, neovascularization on Doppler, possible calcific deposits

high_sensitivity: Pain 2-6 cm proximal to calcaneal insertion (mid-portion) or at insertion
Morning stiffness improving with activity
Tenderness on palpation with pinch compression
VISA-A score < 70
high_specificity: Ultrasound: hypoechoic area, neovascularization on Doppler
MRI: signal change in tendon substance
VISA-A-G ICC = 0.96 (validated German version, rho -0.95 vs. Curwin-Stanish)

clinical_tests.name: Painful arc sign (tendon movement with passive dorsiflexion)

grades.description: Partial rupture (<50% cross-sectional area): Thompson test negative or equivocal, surgical vs. conservative based on MRI findings
Complete rupture: Thompson test positive, palpable gap, complete loss of plantarflexion strength. Conservative: 90-180 days. Surgical: 6-9 months

high_sensitivity: Sudden calf pain with sensation of being struck or kicked
Inability to stand on tiptoe
Palpable gap 2-6cm above calcaneus
Thompson/Simmonds test positive (absent plantarflexion with calf squeeze)
high_specificity: Thompson-Simmonds test: specific for complete rupture
MRI: confirms complete vs. partial and gap length (guides surgical planning)

grades.description: Mild: morning pain resolving within minutes, does not limit activity
Moderate: pain with first steps, persists 15-30 minutes, limits high-impact activity
Severe: pain throughout day, limits walking, may have calcaneal heel spur on X-ray; chronic >6 months

mechanisms: Overuse: repetitive loading of plantar fascia
Pes planus (flat foot) or pes cavus (high arch)

high_sensitivity: Medial calcaneal heel pain, worst with first morning steps
Pain after prolonged rest then initial weight-bearing
Point tenderness at medial calcaneal tubercle
Pain with toe extension (Windlass test)
high_specificity: Windlass test (passive dorsiflexion of first MTP) reproducing heel pain
Ultrasound: plantar fascia thickness >4mm
MRI: signal change at calcaneal insertion

grades.description: Grade 1 MRI: periosteal edema only. Low risk. Return: 2-4 weeks
Grade 2 MRI: periosteal + medullary edema. Low-moderate risk. Return: 4-6 weeks
Grade 3 MRI: periosteal + medullary + cortical involvement. Moderate-high risk. Return: 6-12 weeks
Grade 4 MRI: fracture line visible. High risk (femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, 5th metatarsal = high-risk sites). Return: 12-24 weeks, may require surgery

mechanisms: Cumulative repetitive loading exceeding bone remodeling capacity
Low energy availability / female athlete triad

high_sensitivity: Localized bony tenderness with progressive exertion-related pain
Pain improving with rest
Hop test positive (tibial stress fracture)
Tuning fork vibration pain
high_specificity: MRI (gold standard): periosteal edema + marrow signal change on fat-suppressed sequences
DEXA: low bone mineral density
Bone scan: focal uptake (high sensitivity, lower specificity)

grades.description: Mild: pain after exercise only, diffuse posteromedial tibial tenderness >5cm
Moderate: pain during exercise but not preventing completion; affects up to 20% of runners
Severe: pain preventing exercise; must exclude stress fracture via MRI

high_sensitivity: Diffuse posteromedial tibial pain (>5cm length) with exertion
Pain improving with rest
Tenderness along posteromedial tibial border
Pain with resisted ankle dorsiflexion
high_specificity: MRI: periosteal edema along posteromedial tibia without fracture line (differentiates from stress fracture)
DEXA: low bone density

grades.description: Partial thickness tear: <50% tendon depth involved; GOUTALLIER classification 0-1 (no fatty infiltration)
Partial thickness: >50% tendon depth or small full thickness (<1cm); conservative treatment first
Full thickness tear: Cofield classification small (<1cm), medium (1-3cm), large (3-5cm), massive (>5cm). Surgery often required for athletes. Return 9-12 months post-repair

mechanisms: Overhead throwing (chronic overuse leading to partial tear)
Acute traumatic: heavy lifting or unexpected load

high_sensitivity: Pain with shoulder abduction 60-120 degrees (painful arc)
Pain with overhead activity
Night pain in affected shoulder
Weakness with resisted external rotation
high_specificity: Drop arm test positive (complete tear)
MRI arthrogram (gold standard for partial tears)
Ultrasound (sensitivity 0.87, specificity 0.96 for full-thickness tears)

grades.description: Neer Stage I: edema and hemorrhage of rotator cuff (age <25), reversible with conservative care
Neer Stage II: fibrosis and tendinitis of cuff (age 25-40), usually responds to conservative care
Neer Stage III: bony changes and partial/complete cuff tear (age >40), may require surgery

mechanisms: Weak rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers

high_sensitivity: Neer impingement sign (pain with passive forward flexion)
Hawkins-Kennedy test positive (pain with internal rotation at 90 degrees)
high_specificity: Neer impingement test (pain relief with subacromial lidocaine injection)
MRI/ultrasound: subacromial bursal thickening or cuff changes

grades.description: Snyder Type I: degenerative fraying, biceps anchor intact; typically no surgical intervention
Snyder Type II: biceps anchor detachment (most common, 55-75%); requires repair in overhead athletes; return 4-6 months
Snyder Type III/IV: bucket-handle tear or with biceps extension; typically requires debridement or repair; return 6-9 months

mechanisms: Repetitive overhead throwing (chronic traction on biceps anchor)
Fall on outstretched hand with compression

high_sensitivity: Deep shoulder aching, pain with overhead activities
Painful catching or popping in shoulder
Decreased throwing velocity in pitchers
high_specificity: MRI arthrogram (preferred imaging, though sensitivity varies)
O'Brien active compression test (positive with pain in pronation vs. supination)
Arthroscopy (gold standard)

grades.description: Rockwood Type I: AC ligament sprain only, no displacement, normal radiographs
Rockwood Type II: AC ligament torn, CC ligament sprain; minimal displacement on radiograph
Rockwood Type III-VI: AC + CC ligament disruption, 25-100%+ clavicular elevation; Types IV-VI typically require surgery; Type III controversial

mechanisms: Direct blow to superior or lateral shoulder (fall, tackle)

high_sensitivity: Pain directly over AC joint
AC joint tenderness on palpation
Positive cross-arm adduction test
Palpable AC step deformity (Type III+)
high_specificity: Radiograph: weighted stress views showing clavicular elevation
MRI: useful for Type III classification and CC ligament status
Rockwood classification on radiograph (gold standard)

grades.description: Nirschl Stage 1-2: reversible inflammatory reaction; pain with activity only
Nirschl Stage 3-4: tendinosis (angiofibroblastic degeneration); pain limits activity
Nirschl Stage 5-7: significant tendon disruption or structural failure; may require surgery; chronic >6 months common

mechanisms: Overuse: repetitive wrist extension and gripping
Backhand tennis stroke with poor technique

high_sensitivity: Lateral elbow pain reproduced with wrist extension
Tenderness on palpation at lateral epicondyle / extensor carpi radialis brevis
Pain with resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's test)
high_specificity: Mill's test: pain with forearm pronation + wrist flexion + elbow extension
Cozen's test: pain with resisted wrist extension from pronation
Ultrasound: tendon hypoechogenicity at lateral epicondyle

sport_risk_factors: Tennis (especially recreational players with poor technique)

grades.description: Beck Grade 0-2 CLJ: Labral contusion or minor tear, chondrolabral junction intact or mildly affected. Conservative management appropriate
Beck Grade 3-4 CLJ: Significant tear with chondrolabral junction breakdown; hip arthroscopy if conservative fails. Return 4-6 months post-arthroscopy

mechanisms: Repetitive hip flexion and rotation (dance, gymnastics, martial arts)
Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) - cam or pincer morphology

high_sensitivity: Deep groin or anterior hip pain, often with C-sign
Pain with hip flexion and internal rotation
Clicking or locking sensation in hip
Pain with prolonged sitting
high_specificity: FADIR test (Flexion-Adduction-Internal Rotation): most sensitive clinical test
MRI arthrogram (gold standard, sensitivity 71-90%)
Intra-articular injection: diagnostic and therapeutic

grades.description: Mild: lateral hip pain with prolonged activity, minimal functional limitation
Moderate: pain with walking, stairs, single-leg standing; gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy on imaging
Severe: constant lateral hip/thigh pain, may extend distally; partial or full thickness gluteal tendon tear

mechanisms: Weak hip abductors causing increased tendon load
Compressive loading: crossing legs, side lying on hip

high_sensitivity: Lateral hip pain, greater trochanteric region
Pain with single-leg stance on affected side
Tenderness on palpation of greater trochanter
Pain with hip abduction against resistance
high_specificity: MRI: gluteus medius/minimus tendon signal change at trochanteric insertion
Ultrasound: gluteal tendon hypoechogenicity
IMPORTANT: clinical tests unable to differentiate specific pathoanatomical structure

grades.description: Mild: minor adductor muscle-tendon injury, minimal strength loss, pain with resisted adduction only
Moderate: partial tear, significant pain and weakness with resisted adduction, antalgic gait possible
Severe: complete rupture, avulsion possible; gross weakness and ecchymosis; surgical consultation for complete avulsion

high_sensitivity: Medial groin pain with resisted hip adduction
Pain with passive hip abduction stretch
Tenderness on palpation of adductor longus origin
high_specificity: MRI: confirms grade and location (adductor longus most common)
Ultrasound: fiber disruption at musculotendinous junction

grades.description: Grade I: partial tear, <5mm posterior tibial step-off (normal ~8-10mm); usually managed conservatively
Grade II: complete isolated PCL tear, 5-10mm posterior step-off; conservative first-line for isolated injuries
Grade III: complete PCL with posterolateral corner or other ligament involvement; often requires surgery

mechanisms: Dashboard injury: direct blow to anterior tibia with knee flexed
Fall on flexed knee with plantarflexed foot
Contact: tackle or collision with posterior tibial force

high_sensitivity: Posterior knee pain after direct anterior tibial blow
Posterior sag sign (gravity posterior tibial translation)
Positive posterior drawer test
Vague knee instability on stairs or slopes
high_specificity: Posterior drawer test (most accurate): posterior tibial translation
Quadriceps active test: anterior tibial translation with quad contraction
MRI: PCL signal change (gold standard)

grades.description: Mild: no LOC, symptoms <15 minutes. SCAT5 symptoms score <20. Standard return-to-play protocol days 1-6
Moderate: no LOC, symptoms >15 minutes. Requires medical clearance; postconcussion symptoms may persist
Severe: LOC any duration, prolonged amnesia, or persistent symptoms >7 days. Specialist evaluation; potential prolonged (>1 month) recovery

mechanisms: Direct blow to head (contact sport collision)
Biomechanical force transmitted to brain without direct head contact

high_sensitivity: Any one of: headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, amnesia, LOC after head impact
SCAT5 symptom checklist ≥1 symptom after mechanism
Maddocks questions (inability to recall recent game events)
high_specificity: Graded Symptom Checklist sensitivity 0.89, specificity 1.00
Post-Concussion Scale + ImPACT neurocognitive: sensitivity 0.82, specificity 0.85
Cervical spine and vestibular assessment to differentiate

sport_risk_factors: Previous concussion (significantly increases risk and prolongs recovery)

grades.description: Grade 3-4 MRI: anterior tibial cortex or dreaded black line on X-ray; high-risk fracture requiring non-weight-bearing

mechanisms: Tension stress fracture of anterior tibial cortex
Increased training volume without adequate recovery

high_sensitivity: Focal anterior tibial pain with exertion
Night pain (distinguishes from MTSS)
Dreaded black line on lateral X-ray (specific but late sign)
high_specificity: MRI: Grade 3-4 with cortical involvement
CT scan for precise characterization
DEXA: assess bone mineral density

grades.description: Mild (Flowers-Bhadreshwar Stage 1): pain only with activity, no prominent tuberosity, normal X-ray; typically self-limiting
Flowers Stage 2-3: prominent tibial tuberosity, fragmentation on X-ray, pain limits activity; 3-6 months typical
Flowers Stage 4: ossicle formation, bony prominence; may be chronic until skeletal maturity; rare surgical excision needed

mechanisms: Traction apophysitis at patellar tendon insertion
Repetitive quadriceps contraction during growth spurt
Running, jumping, kicking sports in adolescents

high_sensitivity: Tibial tuberosity pain and swelling in adolescent athlete
Pain with kneeling, jumping, and quadriceps contraction
Point tenderness on tibial tuberosity palpation
Age 10-15 boys, 8-13 girls (correlates with growth spurt)
high_specificity: X-ray: fragmentation of tibial tuberosity apophysis
Ultrasound: patellar tendon thickening at tuberosity insertion
Clinical diagnosis in appropriate age group with classic presentation

injuries.injury_name: Sports-Related Low Back Pain / Lumbar Strain

grades.description: Acute muscular/ligamentous strain: pain <6 weeks, no neurological symptoms; self-limiting
Subacute: pain 6 weeks to 3 months; may have disc involvement on MRI without neurological deficit
Chronic / structural: pain >3 months, disc herniation with radiculopathy or spondylolysis; may require surgery

mechanisms: Repetitive extension loading (gymnastics, cricket fast bowling, volleyball)

high_sensitivity: Lumbosacral pain with activity
Movement-related pain (flexion or extension limited)
Lumbar paraspinal muscle tenderness
high_specificity: Straight leg raise (for disc herniation with radiculopathy): sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.26
SPECT or MRI for spondylolysis (adolescent with extension pain)
Waddell's signs (psychosocial modifiers of poor prognosis)

grades.description: Mild (BAMIC 1): minor fiber disruption at musculotendinous junction or muscle belly, minor calf tightness; MCIC Functional Grade
Moderate (BAMIC 2): significant partial tear at medial gastrocnemius musculotendinous junction (tennis leg); echymosis, antalgic gait
Severe (BAMIC 3-4): complete tear, significant gap palpable; conservative or surgical depending on structure

mechanisms: Sudden dorsiflexion with knee extended (tennis, badminton)

high_sensitivity: Sudden posterior lower leg pain with push-off or explosive movement
Tenderness on palpation of medial gastrocnemius musculotendinous junction
Pain with calf raise or toe-walking
Thompson test negative (distinguishes from Achilles rupture)
high_specificity: Ultrasound: focal hyperechoic area at medial gastrocnemius MTJ
MRI: BAMIC/MCIC grading for return-to-sport decision
Negative Thompson test (intact Achilles)

grades.description: Mild: minor tear, pain with activity, full range of motion, no significant weakness
Moderate: partial tear, pain limits high-intensity activities, possible ecchymosis
Severe: complete tear or avulsion (often rectus femoris at AIIS), gross weakness; avulsions may require surgical fixation

mechanisms: Sudden forced hip extension while flexing
Avulsion: adolescent AIIS avulsion from forceful kick

high_sensitivity: Anterior hip/groin pain with resisted hip flexion
Thomas test: increased hip flexor tightness
Pain with passive hip extension stretch
high_specificity: MRI: signal change at iliopsoas or rectus femoris proximal attachment
Ultrasound: fiber disruption at iliopsoas musculotendinous junction
X-ray: avulsion fragment at AIIS (adolescent athletes)

grades.description: Zone 1 Avulsion: tuberosity avulsion by peroneus brevis or lateral band of plantar fascia; excellent prognosis conservative
Zone 2 Jones fracture: metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction; higher risk of non-union; often managed surgically in athletes
Zone 3 Diaphyseal stress fracture: highest non-union risk; surgery (intramedullary screw) recommended for athletes

high_sensitivity: Lateral foot pain after inversion or direct blow
Point tenderness at base of 5th metatarsal
Ottawa Foot Rules: tenderness at base of 5th MT = X-ray indicated
high_specificity: X-ray: confirms fracture zone and displacement
CT: for surgical planning and union assessment
Ottawa Foot Rules sensitivity 100% for 5th MT fracture

grades.description: Grade I partial: strain without structural failure; conservative treatment; return 6-8 weeks
Grade II: significant partial tear >50% of tendon; conservative or surgical based on athlete demands; return 3-6 months
Grade III complete rupture: complete tendon avulsion typically at humeral insertion; surgical repair recommended for athletes; return 6-9 months

mechanisms: Eccentric overload during bench press (most common in weightlifters)
Forced shoulder extension and external rotation

high_sensitivity: Sudden anterior chest / shoulder pain during bench press or forced extension
Audible pop
Visible deformity or asymmetry of anterior chest
Weakness of adduction and internal rotation
high_specificity: MRI: confirms complete vs. partial tear and retraction distance
Ultrasound: visible gap in pectoralis major tendon
Clinical: loss of anterior axillary fold contour

grades.description: Non-displaced (Herbert Type A/B1): waist or distal pole, stable; cast immobilization 8-12 weeks OR early surgery for athletes
Displaced / proximal pole (Herbert Type B2-D): higher non-union risk; surgical fixation standard for athletes; return 3-6 months

mechanisms: Direct impact to wrist in boxing or martial arts

high_sensitivity: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness (sensitivity 100%, specificity 9%)
Pain with axial load on thumb
Scaphoid tubercle tenderness
high_specificity: MRI: gold standard within 24-48h (sensitivity 98%, specificity 99%)
CT: used if X-ray normal but clinical suspicion high
X-ray: only 65-80% sensitive acutely

diagnostic_confidence_framework.description: Evidence-based confidence scoring for clinical diagnosis without imaging

criteria: Classic mechanism of injury matching injury type
2+ high-sensitivity clinical tests positive
1+ high-specificity clinical test positive
Anatomically consistent symptom location
Consistent onset pattern (acute vs. gradual)
Consistent mechanism
1-2 clinical tests positive but mixed sensitivity/specificity
Some atypical features present
levels.action: Initiate conservative management; consider imaging if no improvement in 2-4 weeks

criteria: Atypical mechanism
Conflicting clinical test results
Non-anatomical pain distribution
Red flags present (bone tenderness suggesting fracture, neurological symptoms)
levels.action: Imaging required before proceeding; refer to physician

red_flags: Night pain at rest (bone pathology, tumor)
Unrelenting pain not modified by position
Ottawa Rules positive (suspected fracture after ankle sprain)

return_to_sport_principles.description: Evidence-based return-to-sport criteria applicable across injury types
criteria: Pain-free at rest AND during sport-specific activities
Full range of motion vs. contralateral side
Strength symmetry >90% vs. contralateral (limb symmetry index)
Successful completion of graduated return-to-sport protocol
Psychological readiness (ACL-specific: ACL-RSI scale)
Sport-specific functional performance tests passed
